About the CPR/First Aid event

CPR/First Aid is a Emergency Preparedness event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing · skills.

Ten in-depth lessons for the two-person HOSA CPR/First Aid event, following the 2026–27 test plan (Basic Life Support 40%, First Aid 60%) and every Round Two skill: adult CPR, adult CPR with an AED and infant CPR for Rescuer 1, and severe bleeding and shock, choking, open fractures, severe burns, heat emergencies, epinephrine auto-injectors and naloxone for Rescuer 2. Built around the AHA and American Red Cross guidelines with chain-of-survival sequencing, AED and tourniquet steps, burn and glucose labs, heat-illness sorting and scenario decisions. Always follow the scenario you are given and state whether your team follows AHA or ARC.

CPR/First Aid lessons

Unit 1 · Foundations and adult BLS

Test plan: BLS general concepts, adult CPR and AED. Skills I and II.

  1. The event, first aid foundations and emergency moves 25 min

    About 350,000 cardiac arrests happen outside hospitals in the United States each year, and most occur at home. Survival depends on bystanders who recognize the emergency, call for help, start CPR and use an AED…

  2. Adult BLS: high-quality CPR with two rescuers (Skill I) 25 min

  3. Adult BLS with an AED, rescue breathing and advanced airways (Skill II) 30 min

Unit 2 · Pediatric BLS and choking

Test plan: child and infant CPR, choking. Skills III and V.

  1. Infant and child BLS (Skill III) 25 min

    In children, cardiac arrest usually follows a breathing problem—choking, drowning, severe asthma or sudden unexpected infant death—rather than a heart rhythm problem. That is why breaths matter so much in pediatric CPR…

  2. Choking and breathing emergencies (Skill V) 30 min

Unit 3 · Injury emergencies

Test plan: First Aid—injury emergencies. Skills IV, VI and VII.

  1. Severe bleeding, wounds and shock (Skill IV) 30 min

    A person with severe bleeding from an arm or leg can bleed to death in less than five minutes—often before an ambulance arrives. Firm, direct pressure and a properly placed tourniquet are skills anyone can learn, and…

  2. Fractures, splinting and head, neck and spine injuries (Skill VI) 30 min

    Falls are the leading cause of injury in older adults, and sports injuries send millions of young people to emergency departments every year. A well-placed splint reduces pain, prevents further damage and can protect…

  3. Burns and electrical and chemical injuries (Skill VII) 35 min

    Burns injure hundreds of thousands of people in the United States each year, many of them young children scalded by hot liquids. The right first aid in the first minutes—cooling the burn and protecting it—reduces pain…

Unit 4 · Environmental and medical emergencies

Test plan: First Aid—environmental and medical emergencies. Skills VIII, IX and X.

  1. Heat, cold and other environmental emergencies (Skill VIII) 25 min

    Extreme heat kills more people in the United States than any other weather hazard, and heat stroke is a leading cause of death in young athletes. Cold, lightning, bites, stings and water are other environmental dangers…

  2. Sudden illness, anaphylaxis and opioid overdose (Skills IX and X) 30 min

Sample CPR/First Aid questions

1. A team reviews data from a 10-minute adult cardiac arrest. Chest compressions were being performed for a total of 7 minutes 30 seconds. Which statement about the team’s chest compression fraction (CCF) is correct?

  1. It is 25%, because CCF measures the time without compressions
  2. It is 75%, which exceeds the AHA goal of at least 70%
  3. It is 75%: above the 60% minimum, below the 80% goal
  4. It is 75%, which is below the AHA minimum of 90%
Show answer

C. It is 75%: above the 60% minimum, below the 80% goal

CCF is the share of total resuscitation time spent doing compressions: 7.5 ÷ 10 = 75%. The AHA calls for a CCF of at least 60% and sets a goal of 80% or higher, so this team should shorten pauses for rhythm checks, switches and ventilation.

2. A first aider begins caring for an injured hiker, then leaves before EMS or another trained person arrives, and the hiker’s condition worsens. Which legal term best describes the first aider’s action?

  1. Implied consent
  2. Battery
  3. Abandonment
  4. Breach of confidentiality
Show answer

C. Abandonment

Once you begin care, you have a duty to continue until someone with equal or higher training takes over, the scene becomes unsafe, or you are physically unable to continue. Leaving earlier is abandonment. Battery is touching a person without consent.

3. Which combination of findings defines exertional heat stroke?

  1. Core temperature above 104 °F (40 °C) with CNS dysfunction
  2. Core temperature above 100.4 °F (38 °C) with heavy sweating and a rapid pulse
  3. Painful muscle spasms with a normal mental status
  4. Pale, clammy skin, thirst and nausea with a normal mental status
Show answer

A. Core temperature above 104 °F (40 °C) with CNS dysfunction

Heat stroke is a core temperature above about 104 °F (40 °C) together with CNS dysfunction such as confusion, slurred speech, seizures or collapse. The skin may still be sweaty in exertional heat stroke, so a change in mental status, not dry skin, is the key sign.
